summary.text:
NEMSA's 21 July 2026 Cabinet report combines a covering paper (provisional 2025/26 outturn plus 2026/27 planning) with three appendices — corporate overheads, service delivery, and the Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 & Prudential Indicators. Everything sits in the single PDF; Appendix 3 carries the loan book, prudential indicators and maturity structure in full. This is a combined-authority reader, not a general-purpose council: no HRA, no schools, no commercial portfolio, and all debt (£113m external) is inherited Tyne and Wear PTE / Tyne Tunnel financing. The MSA took no new external borrowing during 2025/26 and none is signalled for 2026/27.

The story of the year is on the investment side. Interest income came in at £22.445m against a £6.800m revised budget — £15.645m over — driven by an investment book that ran between £400m and £490m across the year at yields still comfortably above bank rate. The Cabinet is being asked to transfer £19.4m of that surplus to a newly-created earmarked Interest Reserve rather than fold it into the revenue base (recommendation 5). §2.2 states the explicit rationale: one-off interest gains should not be built into ongoing revenue, and the reserve funds priority Single Assurance Framework projects. It is one of the clearer worked examples of the mechanic we have read from a combined authority. A LOBO was called in and repaid during the year — £10m off the £45m private-sector line, cutting the weighted rate from 4.38% to 4.21% — but the paper names neither the lender nor whether the call rate was accepted.

PWLB loan-book reconciliation is a CLEAN TIE. Paper §3.5 (Appendix 3) prints PWLB debt at £78.333m at 4.10% average, 25 years. Our file, held under the predecessor name 'NORTH EAST COMBINED AUTHORITY', shows six loans (5 maturity + 1 EIP) totalling £78,333,333 at a weighted 4.1029% — matches to the pound and to a basis point. Balance sheet identity: CFR £176.590m less external debt £113.333m gives £63.257m of un-funded CFR, but the paper prints 'Headroom (Under borrowed)' as £52.590m. The £10.667m gap implies an OLTL balance (finance leases most likely, given the Tyne Tunnel and PTE inheritance) that the paper does not disclose. Presentational: the 'Difference' column in the same §3.13(d) table is the sum of the two rows above it, not the movement of the headroom line itself.

officer.body:
Hi Eleanor,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 21 July Cabinet report ahead of the November Treasury Management Update. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The Interest Reserve mechanic at recommendation 5 is one of the clearer worked examples we've read from a combined authority — the surplus, the ring-fence and the reason for it, all in a single paragraph.

The part I'd start with is the reconciliation. Your Appendix 3 paragraph 3.5 prints PWLB borrowing at £78.333m at 4.10% average over 25 years. Our file — held under the predecessor name North East Combined Authority — carries six loans totalling £78,333,333 at a weighted 4.10%, split five maturity plus one EIP. Ties to the pound and to a basis point. The £0.333m sitting in your under-12m bucket at §3.11(b) is the current-year slice of that EIP; the £5m 5-10y row is a single loan at 1.490% in our file, a very cheap survivor from the Tyne and Wear ITA inheritance.

What the year is really about, though, is the interest income. £22.445m against a £6.800m budget, £15.645m over and £0.970m above the Q3 forecast, from an investment book that ran between £400m and £490m and closed at £451.014m at 4.01%. The £19.4m going into the new earmarked Interest Reserve is the mechanical answer to a real question — how much of that £22.4m is a one-off — and it is the same question several of the councils we've read this year were still working through. Roughly 80% of your book sits inside six months (§3.8), which prices the marginal pound at short rates; today's curve (PWLB notice 314/26, PM fixing 14 August) has the 1-year certainty at 4.95% and the 5-year at 5.34%, with Bank Rate at 3.75%. What the MPC does next moves the yield on £451m directly.

The LOBO called in and repaid during 2025/26 (§3.5) is the other line worth naming. £10m off a £45m private-sector position in one year is a material change, and it makes NEMSA the second combined-authority reader in the library with a LOBO story this quarter. The pattern across the councils we've read is that lenders are pushing rate resets and councils are almost always refusing — Dexia at Kent and Tameside in the same window, KBC at Bath and North East Somerset gone floating with six-monthly resets, refused calls at Harrow, Wolverhampton, Staffordshire, Newport, York and Bridgend, an active negotiated run-off at Lewisham. A repaid call at par is the middle answer, and worth having on the file.

For where to look, pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows every council's monthly PWLB draws with rate and maturity — including the councils sitting on the borrowing side of your £105m of inter-authority investments. And pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices any council's PWLB book against the DMO's repayment curve daily. Indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and we don't model MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, three look relevant. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, given your position sits at £52.590m under-borrowed against a £176.590m CFR (§3.13.d) and the shape of that arithmetic moves with the curve. LOBO loans, given how live the topic is in your book and the sector. And the liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look ahead of the forthcoming CIPFA Prudential and Treasury Code updates. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
